title: The Great Umbrella Flip-Flop Fiasco
markdown:
It was a soggy-toast kind of day in Oakhaven. Rain drummed on the windows like tiny tapping fingers. The umbrellas were having a terrible time. On the corner by Market Square, every last one — even Mrs. Higgins’s, the one with the yellow ducklings — did a flip-flop. Pop. Whump. Fzzzt. Inside out they went, like startled jellyfish.

Oakhaven had Milo. Milo could fix anything with gears and wheels. On his shoulder sat Fenn, a clever rook with eyes like little black buttons that missed nothing.

“Caw,” Fenn said, jabbing his beak toward the umbrella chaos. He hopped.

Milo squinted. “You’re right. It’s as if they’re being tickled by a giant feather duster.” He rather liked a puzzle that popped.

“Adventure time, then.”

Fenn ruffled. “Caw,” which Milo took to mean: Lead on. I am extremely ready.

They followed the trail of inside-out umbrellas down a narrow lane: a striped one hugging a lamp-post, a black one in a puddle like a defeated bat, Mrs. Higgins’s ducklings pointing accusingly at the sky. A whoosh grew louder and pulled them toward the old hat shop, Fanciful Fashions and Feathered Hats, closed for years, its sign creaking like a door that had opinions.

The wind pushed. Milo leaned into it. His own umbrella flapped as if it wanted a career change. Fenn nearly took off like a small black kite.

Fenn, with a sharp caw, nudged a loose shutter. A faint whir, like a sleepy bumblebee, leaked from the crack.

“You found it, you brilliant bird.”

Milo pushed the shutter. It shrieked. Inside, the shop was piled with forgotten hats: felt mountains, a veil like a cobweb that had gone to a party, a topper so tall it looked embarrassed.

At the back stood a contraption that might have been dreamt up by someone who had never been told no. Old fans, bicycle wheels, tangled wires — a miniature hurricane, magnificent and slightly wonky.

“A homemade wind tunnel.” Milo tasted dust and oil. Perhaps the owner, Mr. Silas Snoodle, had forgotten the off switch. Or the machine had decided to play a cheeky trick of its own.

The wind inside tugged his hair. If they left it, every hat in Oakhaven would emigrate.

“We need to turn it off.”

Fenn swooped, brave as a very small admiral, and landed on a rusty lever at the base. “Caw.” The off-switch, clearly. The only problem was the gale between Milo and the lever, which had no interest in being reasonable.

Hats whipped around their ears like frantic confetti. Milo’s knees considered a wobble. Then he looked at Fenn, button-eyes bright, waiting.

He spotted a long, sturdy coat rack.

“Grab this. Teamwork.”

Fenn gripped one end in his beak. Milo took the other. They edged toward the churning machine as if crossing a roaring invisible sea. Milo pushed the rack forward like a ship’s prow. The air buffeted. A bowler tried to escape through the shutter and thought better of it.

The rack’s end bumped the rusty lever.

“Push.”

Fenn heaved. Milo shoved. For a moment nothing happened, which was rude of the lever. Then, with a protesting squeak, it moved.

Whoosh. Sputter. Cough. Whirr. Clunk.

Silence arrived, peaceful as a warm mug.

The wind died. Hats settled. The rain outside seemed to sigh.

Milo ruffled Fenn’s feathers. Fenn nudged his cheek, a beakful of victory and friendship.

They stepped back into the gentle rain. Oakhaven’s umbrellas still hung inside out, sad deflated mushrooms along the square. Mrs. Higgins’s ducklings looked seasick but hopeful. Soon someone would shake them right-side out. In the hat shop, the bicycle wheels were only bicycle wheels again, and Mr. Silas Snoodle’s machine, at last, remembered how to be still.
